summary:
Swapping two neighbours that are out of order fixes exactly one out-of-order pair and changes no other pair, so
the fewest swaps equals the number of out-of-order pairs (inversions). Count them with merge sort in
O(n log n); the answer can exceed 2³¹, so use 64-bit.

question.md:
Sort students by height using only swaps of **neighbours**. Equal heights can be in either order. Return the
minimum number of swaps.

- **Up to 10⁵ students:** up to ~5 × 10⁹ swaps, which needs a 64-bit result.

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- Equal heights may stay in either order, so equal pairs never need a swap.
- Already sorted: 0.
- The count reaches about `n²/2 = 5 × 10⁹`: use 64 bits.

think.md:
**Counting pairs with merge sort.** Questions like "how many pairs `i < j` have `a[i] > a[j]`" split nicely:

- pairs with both positions in the **left half** and pairs in the **right half** are counted recursively;
- pairs that **cross** (`i` in the left half, `j` in the right half) only care about the *values*, not their order
  inside each half, so both halves may be sorted first, and with sorted halves the crossing pairs are counted with a
  linear sweep.

Each level of the recursion does O(n) counting plus O(n) merging, over `log n` levels: **O(n log n)** instead of O(n²).

**Why neighbour swaps = out-of-order pairs.** Swapping two neighbours changes the relative order of exactly
those two students and no one else. If they were out of order, the number of out-of-order pairs drops by exactly
one; otherwise it rises by one. The sorted line has zero out-of-order pairs, so at least that many swaps are
needed, and bubble sort shows that many suffice (it only ever swaps out-of-order neighbours).

For `[3, 1, 2, 5, 4, 2]` there are 6 out-of-order pairs, so **6** swaps.

idea.md: Bubble sort, counting every swap. Each swap fixes exactly one out-of-order pair, so the count is the answer.

lines.text: A copy and the swap counter (64-bit).
Each pass bubbles the largest remaining value to the end.
Swap only out-of-order neighbours: each swap removes exactly one inversion.

walk.title: Bubble sort, counting swaps: each swap of two neighbours fixes exactly one out-of-order pair.

limits.md: Performs every swap one by one; counting inversions with merge sort gives the same number in O(n log n).

idea.md: Count inversions with merge sort (add `mid − i` whenever a right value is taken). That count is the minimum number of neighbour swaps.

lines.text: A copy to sort and a merge buffer.
Inversions inside each half, counted recursively (64-bit counts).
Merge; equal heights don't count (`<=`), since they may stay in either order.
The right front jumps ahead of every value still in the left half: one inversion with each.
Finish the merge, copy back, return this range's count.

steps.text: Merge [1] with [2]: each time the right side's front is smaller, it beats every value still waiting on the left. +0.
Merge [3] with [1, 2]: each time the right side's front is smaller, it beats every value still waiting on the left. +2.
Merge [4] with [2]: each time the right side's front is smaller, it beats every value still waiting on the left. +1.
Merge [5] with [2, 4]: each time the right side's front is smaller, it beats every value still waiting on the left. +2.
Merge [1, 2, 3] with [2, 4, 5]: each time the right side's front is smaller, it beats every value still waiting on the left. +1.

walk.title: Count inversions with merge sort instead of performing the swaps.

takeaways.md:
- **Minimum adjacent swaps to sort = number of inversions.**
- Each adjacent swap changes the inversion count by exactly one.
- **Pitfall:** counting equal heights as inversions.
